items.en: The Edge brings Fitbit’s screen-equipped offerings up to speed with better health tracking, a brighter display, and improved durability. After testing it, I’m still not ready to give up my Fitbit Air.
Google’s first repairable tracker. A bigger screen with adjustable brightness. More advanced health metrics and workout tracking.
Band fastening can be finicky. Auto-pause can be overly sensitive. No Google Wallet.

Earlier this year, the Google Fitbit Air won me over and made me wonder why I ever wanted a display on my fitness tracker in the first place. Of course, not everyone is ready to quit the screen cold turkey, especially if your wearable doubles as your everyday smartwatch. Google Fitbit hasn’t introduced a new tracker with a screen since 2023, and the older models are starting to fall behind on health features and hardware. That deters both newcomers who want a screen and longtime users who have to choose among aging models.

At $180, the new Google Fitbit Edge costs $20 more than Fitbit's Charge 6 ($160) and $80 more than the screenless Air ($100), but far less than Google's Pixel Watch 5 ($400). After 12 days of testing, I’d recommend it to Fitbit owners looking to upgrade. Personally, though, the Edge hasn’t given me enough reasons to give up my Fitbit Air.

The Edge is comfortable enough to wear throughout the day and overnight. Its dimensions are slightly larger than the Charge 6’s (39.2 x 25.5 x 11.5 mm versus 36.73 x 23.09 x 11.20 mm), but I found the capsule shape sat more naturally on my wrist than its predecessor’s rectangular build. It feels like a better option for people with slimmer wrists and those who might find the Pixel Watch or Apple Watch too bulky to sleep with.

As with any smartwatch, comfort also depends on the band. The Edge comes with Google’s Active Band, which is fine for workouts but isn’t my favorite of the available options. Google also offers the HNBR (high-performance synthetic elastomer) Active Sport, the breathable Performance Loop, the silicone Magnet band, and the Metal Links band.

I found myself alternating between the Metal Links and Performance Loop. I love the look of the former for a night out or a more formal setting, and the latter is best for everyday wear. The Performance Loop’s micro-adjustable fit makes it easy to get a precise fit, but it's just as easy to pull it a little too tight. I also noticed that the band occasionally popped loose while I was adjusting it. The tracker was still attached from one side, so I wasn’t worried about losing it, but the fastening mechanism didn’t feel as secure as it should. I eventually noticed that the locking button was stuck and had to fiddle with the mechanism to fix the issue.

The 1.34-inch display is the Edge’s obvious advantage over the screenless Air. I noticed the difference most during workouts. On outdoor runs, I could check my metrics and control my music without slowing down. The display also reaches roughly twice the Charge’s maximum brightness, making it easier to read in direct sunlight. With Google Maps integration, I could follow turn-by-turn directions from my wrist while running or cycling, without having to pull out my phone.

I do prefer Wear OS’s more colorful interface; Fitbit’s watch faces also feel a little elementary by comparison. But Fitbit’s software offers up to seven days of battery life, which is a feature the Pixel Watch can’t match. The Edge is also compatible with both iOS and Android, unlike the Pixel Watch. Plus, in a first for Fitbit, the Edge is Google’s first repairable fitness tracker, with modular construction including a replaceable battery, matching the Pixel Watch. This is likely due to battery regulations set to take effect next year in the European Union, which will require removable and replaceable batteries in smartphones, smartwatches, and similar devices starting February 18, 2027.

The Edge is a significant upgrade over the Charge 6 when it comes to health and fitness capabilities. Google has added more detailed workout metrics and a few hardware upgrades that make the Edge a more capable fitness tracker.

Some of the additions are aimed at long-term health tracking. Like the Pixel Watch 5 and the Air, the Edge offers monthly blood pressure and insulin resistance trends. Its SpO2 readings now include nightly averages, ranges, and changes over time. There’s also 24/7 heart rate tracking, cardio load metrics, and an updated ECG app with atrial fibrillation (AFib) detection. Alongside nutrition logging, if you use a continuous glucose monitor (CGM), you can view glucose insights.

Like any Google wearable, most features are locked behind Google Health Premium, which costs $10 per month or $100 annually. Without the subscription, you still get the core metrics and scores, but the deeper analysis and AI coaching are inaccessible. In other words, the Google Health Premium membership is essential to the experience. (Buying any new device gets you a three-month trial.)

The hardware has also caught up to Google’s latest models. A barometric altimeter measures elevation changes and floors climbed. The Edge also finally gets an IP68 rating for dust and water resistance. Its display brings more of these metrics to your watch face, including live workout data and visual guidance.

Google adds a gyroscope that improves automatic activity recognition, but it may have overcorrected a little. During outdoor runs, the Edge auto-paused when I stopped and resumed when I started moving again. At times, it was too sensitive; even taking a single step forward while catching my breath sometimes restarted my workout. It’s not a major downside, but worth noting that I sometimes had to correct the Edge’s decisions.

The Charge 6 supports contactless payments, but the Edge doesn’t, which feels like a regression for a newer model. If you want to use the Edge as a smartwatch, the lack of NFC technology is disappointing. I didn’t miss it much myself because I rarely leave home without my phone, but it’s a beloved feature that shouldn’t have disappeared without good reason.

The Fitbit Edge is a robust smartwatch, and Charge 6 owners will be happy with the improvements. I’m less convinced it’ll win over newcomers. The Fitbit Air remains the most appealing value in Google’s lineup, and the Edge doesn’t offer much more to change that. Without NFC for contactless payment, it feels like a smartwatch with one too many compromises.

Anthropic has officially filed the prospectus for its initial public offering, which means the AI lab has put all kinds of formerly private information on display. While the prospectus contains the eye-popping revenue—and even larger expenditures—you might expect, the biggest section of the filing by far is given over to “risk factors,” which are all the things that could squash Anthropic’s big plans. Or, in this case, humanity itself.

While much has been made about the extent to which AI represents an existential threat to humankind, the specific mechanisms by which it could bring about that destruction are largely opaque. If nothing else, the 94 pages that Anthropic’s prospectus devotes to risk factors make clear both where it sees the danger coming from, and the ways in which its researchers are running toward it in order to win the AI arms race.

“Sufficiently advanced AI systems could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity,” the prospectus reads, citing concerns both from critics and regulators and from inside Anthropic itself. (It’s the first of three times the phrase “existential risks” pops up.)
Anthropic is careful to tie that outcome, though, to a specific process: recursive self-improvement.

The idea behind RSI is strikingly simple. It describes a state in which humans hand over the research and development of AI models to other AI models. AI already plays a big role here—and at least one lab has used something close to RSI to speed up development on a model that punches above its weights—but the scenario that sparks doomsday talk is one in which humans are no longer in the loop at all.

Or, as the Anthropic filing puts it: “Risks will increase as AI systems substantially automate AI research and development if, for example, they accelerate AI progress beyond our ability to evaluate and safeguard new models.”

The prospectus repeatedly makes the point that RSI could lead to AI models that develop faster than the company’s safeguards, and that the company may not even realize it has lost that race until it’s too late. Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

It also gets specific about what might happen after that. “As AI systems become more autonomous and capable of taking consequential actions with less human oversight,” the prospectus says, “there is a risk that such systems could, whether due to misalignment with human intentions, errors in objective specification, or self-preserving behaviors, take harmful actions independently and at scale without human intervention.” This is Skynet territory.

Speaking of robots, Anthropic flags concerns about those as well. “When our models direct physical equipment,” the filing says, “errors, misaligned behavior, adversarial manipulation, or misuse could result in bodily injury, property damage, damage to costly equipment or experimental materials, or the release of hazardous substances, and such consequences may be immediate and irreversible.”

You might think, given the apparently existential stakes, that serious consideration would be given to whether RSI should be pursued at all, much less embraced. In an industry as competitive as frontier AI, though, it’s become fait accompli. Here’s how Anthropic describes that same process elsewhere in the prospectus, this time in a section about the startup’s “core advantages:”
“We refer to this recursive dynamic as ‘closing the loop,’” the prospectus says, “and we believe it is one of the most significant structural advantages in frontier AI.”

Failure to “close the loop,” Anthropic later says, could result in “falling progressively further behind as competitors continuously use AI to further enhance their own development capabilities.” In other words, the same systems that are causing all that existential concerns are the ones Anthropic sees as critical to its success.

Every AI company is dealing with this same tension. When former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon went viral for loudly resigning, he put curbing RSI at the top of his wish list for the industry. Employees at Google DeepMind and elsewhere have had similar revelations. There are multiple bills in Congress, including one cosponsored by Bernie Sanders, that propose a ban on RSI. At the same time, these are for-profit companies, and there are trillions of dollars at stake.
It’s a tricky dynamic to navigate. Recursive self-improvement could become a runaway train that destroys humanity. But until then, just look at how fast it can go.
Anthropic filed key paperwork on Monday ahead of a highly anticipated initial public offering, providing new details about its finances and the risks facing its business.

According to the filing, the artificial intelligence company plans to go public on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT. The IPO could come later in November, The Wall Street Journal reported. The S-1 prospectus does not include details on how much the company plans to raise or its targeted valuation; The New York Times reported in August that it was looking to raise more than $100 billion with a valuation around $2 trillion.

“The advent of machine intelligence is one of the seminal moments in human history,” Anthropic wrote in the filing. “We encourage you, as a prospective owner of our stock, not to think of your purchase in purely transactional terms. We hope you will see it instead as an opportunity to be part of something greater.”

The paperwork offers a window into the company’s finances through the first half of 2026. Its revenue grew to more than $16 billion, up from about $4.5 billion in 2025. The Claude maker emphasized its growing enterprise business, noting that more than 11,900 customers spent at least $100,000 in the past twelve months; more than 1,900 spent $1 million or more; and roughly 250 customers spent $10 million or more.
Despite its growing revenue, Anthropic has yet to turn a profit. It posted a net loss of $80.7 billion in the first half of 2026, compared to a net loss of $13 billion in the same period last year.

While it’s expected that a company accurately reports its risk factors, the prospectus also features a particularly thorough list of potential business quagmires, noting that investing in the stock carries “a high degree of risk.”
Those risks range from the ability to secure adequate compute to intense competition from rival labs to advanced AI systems’ potential to “pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.”

The filing warns about the possibility that sophisticated AI could be abused by threat actors to launch cyberattacks and develop novel biological weapons, or by authoritarian governments to surveil their citizens. Anthropic also pointed to the risk that it could lose control of the AI models it develops.
It also highlighted the volatility of government action, specifically noting the Trump administration’s decision to designate the company as a supply chain risk.

“While we continue to work with government agencies, we cannot be certain that the resolution of these lawsuits will not adversely affect our ability to sell to government agencies and other customers that sell products and services to the US government, and in turn adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations,” the filing concluded.

In September, Anthropic’s rival OpenAI—which filed confidentially for IPO in the summer—announced that it no longer intended to go public this year, citing concerns over the risks posed to humanity by AI.

Anthropic was founded in 2021 by seven former employees of OpenAI, who had reportedly lost faith in the lab’s ability to develop advanced AI models safely. Anthropic markets itself as highly safety-conscious; its CEO, Dario Amodei, has repeatedly commented on the risk that AI could eliminate scores of jobs, and act against human interests.
The filings also outline Anthropic’s ambition to develop sophisticated AI models capable of accelerating scientific discovery, curing disease, and spurring economic growth.
“To build AI is to harness cognition itself, and anything so powerful can be used for ill as well as good,” the company wrote.
The company did not immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment.

As the Milwaukee Brewers and Tampa Bay Rays face off in the 2026 World Series, there’s more than baseball on the line. In addition to the Commissioner’s Trophy, the two teams are playing for works of fine art.

The Milwaukee Museum of Art and Museum of Fine Arts in St. Petersburg, Florida, have agreed to a friendly wager: The museum from the losing team’s city will send a Claude Monet painting from its collection to the winner’s museum, where it will have a “victory lap in the galleries,” per a statement from the Milwaukee Museum of Art.

“When I moved to Milwaukee, I became a part of the Brew Crew,” Kim Sajet, director of the Milwaukee Art Museum, says in the statement. “They’re the best team in baseball, and I’m backing them with one of our most beloved paintings. Two Monets will look incredible in our galleries … Go Brewers!”

Klaudio Rodriguez, executive director and CEO of the Museum of Fine Arts, St. Petersburg, responds: “We admire Kim’s enthusiasm, but we think Milwaukee’s Monet would enjoy a little Florida vacation. We’re backing the Rays all the way, and we’re ready to welcome Milwaukee’s masterpiece to St. Petersburg. Let’s see Milwaukee put its Monet where its mouth is.”

The Brewers currently enjoy a 2-0 series lead ahead of Game 3 in Tampa Bay on Monday night. If they win two more games and emerge victorious, the “Brew Crew” will welcome St. Petersburg’s Houses of Parliament: Effect of Fog, London to its galleries.

Created in 1904, the painting depicts the Palace of Westminster with two silhouetted boats in the River Thames on a grey London day. It is among the more than one hundred canvases and 20 pastels that Monet produced of the Thames around the turn of the 20th century. The London series is the artist’s second-largest, behind only his Water Lilies collection, which comprises nearly 300 canvases.

While Monet was creating his Thames paintings, he insisted on keeping the group of works cohesive. “I cannot send you a single canvas of London,” Monet wrote to his art dealer Paul Durand-Ruel in 1903. “It is indispensable to have them all before me, and to tell the truth not one is definitely finished. I develop them all together.”

The final paintings are today spread apart in collections across the world, but no matter which team wins their first World Series title, two of Monet’s Thames paintings will be reunited, at least temporarily.

If the Rays stage a comeback, the art museum in St. Petersburg—the city on the Tampa Bay where the Rays play—will exhibit the Milwaukee Art Museum’s only Monet: Waterloo Bridge, Sunlight Effect, dated to 1903.

Depicting the Thames glistening with sunlight and dark plumes of smoke emitting from factories in the background, the piece is one of Monet’s many depictions of the Waterloo bridge, which he painted at different times of day, from foggy sunrise to clearer sunset.

To work on his London series—composed of views of the House of Parliament, Waterloo Bridge and Charing Cross Bridge—Monet traveled from Paris to London via train and boat. His first trip across the English Channel came in 1870, to avoid conscription in the Franco-Prussian War.

Monet made multiple trips to London in the late 1890s and the early 1900s. He painted the two bridges from his room’s balcony at the Savoy Hotel and painted the Houses of Parliament from St. Thomas’ Hospital in the afternoons. Painting the same scenes over and over offered the painter ample opportunity to experiment with weather and light, to see the subtlest of shifts.
“I adore London; it’s a mass, a whole, and it’s so simple. But what I love more than anything in London is the fog,” Monet told art dealer René Gimpel in 1920.
Both Houses of Parliament and Waterloo Bridge are currently on view at their respective institutions. The details of the winning loan will be announced after the World Series concludes.

In 2003, baseball historian John Thorn discovered the first known reference to the game of baseball: a 1791 law from Pittsfield, Massachusetts, banning people from playing too close to the new town meeting house.

Art museums have taken up friendly sports betting in recent years. In 2023, the Philadelphia Museum of Art sent a painting by Thomas Eakins to the Nelson-Atkins Museum of Art in Kansas City, after the Kansas City Chiefs beat the Philadelphia Eagles in the Super Bowl. After the Eagles won the 2025 rematch, Kansas City sent an Édouard Manet painting to Philadelphia.

This isn’t the first time that the Milwaukee Art Museum has engaged in a championship bet. In 2011, when the Green Bay Packers beat the Pittsburgh Steelers in the Super Bowl, the institution received Pierre-Auguste Renoir’s Bathers With Crab, painted circa 1890-1899, from the Carnegie Museum of Art, and exhibited the work for three months.

“The game was certainly a nail-biter!” the Pittsburgh museum posted to social media after the Steelers' defeat. “And true to our word, the beautiful Renoir will have a short vacation in the Milwaukee Art Museum galleries. Wonder who we’ll be wagering with next year?”
The world’s shallow-water coral reefs are in trouble: If climate change continues unchecked, most of these vital ecosystems could collapse within the next 50 years, experts predict.

On October 22, the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s Red List of Ecosystems released its first global assessment of shallow-water reefs. The findings paint a grim picture. Coral reefs in 122 of the 127 tropical and subtropical ecoregions they looked at—96 percent—are critically endangered, meaning they’re at extremely high risk of collapse by 2075.

The list of critically endangered ecoregions includes the Great Barrier Reef off Australia, the Coral Triangle in the western Pacific Ocean and the Mesoamerican Barrier Reef System in the Caribbean, just to name a few. Four of the analyzed ecoregions had too little reef data for researchers to determine their statuses.
Even if some coral species manage to survive a broader ecosystem collapse, they could end up being too far apart from one another to reproduce, preventing them from rebuilding their populations.

“If the population size gets so small that you don’t have another coral to mate with nearby, then reproductive failure will happen,” James Guest, a marine ecologist at Newcastle University in England, tells New Scientist’s Alec Luhn. “That species is in what’s called an extinction vortex.”

Coral reefs are built by tiny coral animals called polyps, which produce hard limestone skeletons that accumulate over time to form reef structures. Most reef-building corals live in partnership with colorful, microscopic algae that reside in their tissues and use sunlight to make food, providing the corals with much of the energy they need to survive.

When corals get stressed, particularly when ocean temperatures get too hot, they can expel their algae partners. This process, known as bleaching, turns the corals bone-white and leaves them without a primary food source. If the stressful conditions persist, the corals can eventually starve to death.

Earlier this month, researchers reported that a sick coral fragment can heal with the help of a ‘magic touch’ from a healthy, genetically identical piece. Most individual corals are colonies of cloned polyps.

The assessment found that heat stress resulting from climate change is the primary threat to coral reef ecosystems around the world. Rising ocean temperatures and marine heat waves are causing mass bleaching events, turning once-vibrant communities into barren underwater wastelands. Overfishing and pollution also threaten the world’s reefs, which support roughly a quarter of all marine species and help provide food, jobs and protection for people in coastal communities.

So far, just one of the world’s shallow-water coral reef ecosystems has collapsed, according to the IUCN: the one near the western Galápagos Islands. Those reefs lost more than 95 percent of their coral after the devastating 1982-83 El Niño event, which caused dramatic warming in the eastern Pacific, among other problems.

Still, bleaching events seem to be becoming more frequent and intense because of climate change—and scientists worry they’re now occurring so frequently that reef ecosystems don’t have time to recover between them.

“Reefs are like Picasso paintings under water,” Ben Fitzpatrick, a marine scientist with the University of Western Australia Oceans Institute who led the assessment on Australia’s coral reef ecosystems, tells the Guardian’s Graham Readfearn. “They have all these wonderful inhabitants in their millions. You can spend a lifetime trying to understand how all these weird critters go about their daily lives. To think we might lose that is devastating.”

Though the outlook is bleak, the scientists behind the new report emphasized that all hope is not lost. Their findings are based on the current “middle-of-the-road” warming projections—but if the world curbs greenhouse gas emissions, the situation could improve. Without the effects of future climate change, the researchers say just 24 percent of the reef ecosystems would be critically endangered, instead of nearly all.

“This must be a wake-up call rather than a cause for despair,” Mishal Gudka, a conservation biologist at the University of Melbourne in Australia who served as scientific lead for the assessment, says in a statement. “Coral reefs have shown a remarkable ability to bounce back from devastating bleaching events. Pockets of surviving, resilient coral reefs can still remain in the future, so we must do everything within our reach to set them up for success.”

Scientists are exploring innovative ways to help corals better withstand warming oceans, from cooling and shading reefs to breeding more heat-tolerant varieties. These methods may be helpful, but they likely won’t be enough to save the world’s coral reefs on their own.

“In the intervention and restoration community, I think we all recognize that it’s not going to matter unless climate change is addressed and greenhouse gas emissions are addressed,” John Parkinson, a marine ecologist at the University of South Florida, tells the New York Times’ Catrin Einhorn.

Western Europe faced its hottest summer ever this year. And it was the third toastiest summer on record for the entire continent, which is warming faster than any other. Now, scientists have calculated a death toll from the season’s sweltering temperatures: more than 50,000 people across the continent’s cities.

The estimate, which has not yet been peer-reviewed but is slated to be published in the journal Nature Health, marks a new record for heat-related deaths in Europe, nearly doubling the toll of the last two deadliest summers in 2022 and 2003. About two-thirds of the deaths are directly attributable to climate change, mainly driven by the burning of fossil fuels.

“I think we can be quite confident in stating that the summer of 2026 is likely to have been the worst on record for heat-related mortality across much of Europe,” says study co-author Clair Barnes, a climate scientist at Imperial College London, to Laura Paddison at CNN.

During the spring and summer, Europe faced an assault of back-to-back heat waves. The hot, dry conditions also contributed to intense wildfires that threatened lives across the region. However, much of the infrastructure in Western and Northern Europe wasn’t designed to cope with the sweltering temperatures brought on by human-caused global warming, Barnes explains to Seth Borenstein at the Associated Press.

To estimate heat deaths, governments will usually look through death records to identify excess mortalities that may be attributed to higher temperatures, Warren Cornwall reports for Science. In this study, however, Barnes and her colleagues took a different approach. They used published peer-reviewed research to build computer simulations of how many people would have died between June and August both with and without the effects of climate change. They specifically looked at deaths in 854 urban areas across 30 countries.

Analyses revealed that 50,391 deaths in those cities could be attributed to higher temperatures. Nearly one-third of the deaths occurred between June 17 and July 1, when a heat wave brought temperatures 9.5 degrees Fahrenheit above the average temperature in 1991 to 2020.

The summer was especially deadly for people ages 85 and up, who represent about 22,500—nearly 45 percent—of the mortalities. But young people were also affected, with people between 20 and 44 representing more than 800 of the deaths.
The researchers didn’t even include deaths related to excessive springtime heat, which they estimate killed about 1,500 people between May 21 and 31.

The numbers are likely an underestimate, says Kristie Ebi, a climate epidemiologist at the University of Washington who wasn’t involved in the study, to Science. Computer models often assume that deaths rise at a steady rate with growing temperatures, but it’s possible that fatalities actually shoot up during the most extreme heat.

Other scientists who weren’t involved in the study, however, believe the estimates should be interpreted with caution. They “involve several uncertainties and assumptions,” says Lasse Vestergaard, an epidemiologist and chief physician at the European Mortality Monitoring Network, to CNN, though they largely align with his group’s estimates.

As climate change continues to raise temperatures, experts stress that more needs to be done to address extreme heat. “We can’t just be mopping up the mess on the floor without thinking about turning the faucet off,” says Jonathan Patz, a global health researcher at the University of Wisconsin-Madison who wasn’t involved in the work, to the AP.

“So, we need prevention at different levels. We need better cooling and protecting vulnerable populations from inevitable increased frequency and extreme heat waves. But we also need to go to the root of the problem and absolutely address the burning of fossil fuels.”

A neglected "ghost particle" may have dominated the universe right after the Big Bang — changing how the cosmos expanded in its first moments and reshaping the conditions under which matter won out over antimatter, a new study suggests. In other words, it may explain why anything exists at all.

The particle, a hypothetical "right-handed" neutrino, briefly could have held more energy than everything else in the infant universe combined, which would have sped up cosmic expansion and delayed key particle interactions, the study proposes. The research was published Sept. 8 in the journal Physical Review Letters.

Neutrinos are ghostly particles that rarely interact with anything. A typical neutrino from the sun could pass through a slab of lead a light-year thick — about 5.9 trillion miles (9.5 trillion kilometers) — before striking a single atom. Neutrinos come in three types, or "flavors," and switch between them as they travel, making use of a subtle quantum effect that works only if they have mass. Yet the Standard Model of particle physics predicts they should be massless.

One popular fix involves "right-handed" neutrinos. Particles spin a bit like tiny tops, and physicists call them left- or right-handed depending on how they spin relative to their direction of travel. A right-handed particle rotates like an ordinary screw being driven in, turning clockwise as it moves away from you. Every neutrino detected so far is left-handed and turns counterclockwise as it flies away, like a screw with a reverse thread.

"Right-handed neutrinos are hypothetical particles that do not feel the weak nuclear force, "unlike their left-handed counterparts, which are part of the Standard Model," study co-author Rishav Roshan, a theoretical physicist at the University of Southampton in the U.K., told Live Science via email. "They are characterized by having no electric charge and being much heavier."
"Right-handed neutrinos may mix with left-handed neutrinos, helping to explain the mass of the latter" and why they switch flavors, Roshan said.

In quantum physics, particles that mix can exist as a blend of two identities at once. In a theoretical framework called the seesaw mechanism, each ordinary neutrino carries a faint trace of a heavy right-handed partner, and that trace gives it a tiny mass. The heavier the partner, the fainter the trace and the lighter the ordinary neutrino — hence the name, after the playground ride whose ends move in opposite directions.

The particles could solve other puzzles, too. They "aim to address several issues, including the origin of neutrino masses, the matter-antimatter asymmetry of the universe, and the nature of dark matter," Roshan said.

The Big Bang should have made equal amounts of matter and antimatter, which would have annihilated each other, forbidding the universe as we know it from ever taking shape. Right-handed neutrinos play a crucial role in models' proposals that the "observed matter-antimatter imbalance arose from processes involving these neutrinos in the early universe," Roshan said.
In this picture, decaying heavy neutrinos left behind a slight excess of leptons — the particle family that includes electrons — that later became today's surplus of matter, he explained.

The seesaw framework usually includes three right-handed neutrinos, but because two are enough to explain the data, physicists often ignore the third, assuming it is too heavy or interacts too feebly with matter.

In the new study, Roshan and Sudipta Show, a physicist at the Indian Institute of Technology Kanpur, examined what this neglected particle — which, in the team's main example, was about 100 trillion times as heavy as a proton — would have done after the Big Bang.

At first, the particle would have zipped around at nearly light speed, so its energy would have faded like that of light, which would have both spread out and stretched to weaker wavelengths as space expanded. But as the cosmos cooled, the particle would have slowed down and most of its energy would have become locked in its mass, which would have been only spread out. Its share of the cosmic energy therefore would have grown until it dominated, and the long-lived particle would have stayed in charge until it decayed into other particles, according to the team's computations.

The study reveals that the neglected right-handed neutrino "significantly impacts the early universe's expansion dynamics, driving a period of early matter domination," Roshan said. This change "affects various Standard Model interactions" that could help to explain the matter-antimatter asymmetry, Roshan added.

Each interaction would have switched on only once it outpaced the expansion of space. Because a universe dominated by the heavy neutrino would have expanded faster, the interactions would have had to wait until it cooled further.

These interactions would have let the early universe distinguish lepton flavors, which would have affected how the matter surplus formed. Thanks to the delay, the team found, a lighter right-handed neutrino about 100 billion times as heavy as a proton could have produced the observed amount of matter before the flavors could be told apart — even after the heavy neutrino's decay diluted part of it.
The heavy neutrino is far too massive to create in any particle accelerator, so tests must be indirect.

Gravitational waves — ripples in space-time — offer one such route. An era dominated by the heavy neutrino would have left a telltale kink in the background of early-universe gravitational waves, such as those from "cosmic strings" — hypothetical thread-like defects in space. The results can be tested through forthcoming facilities such as the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) and the Square Kilometer Array Observatory (SKAO), Roshan noted.

LISA, a space-based European Space Agency mission, is scheduled to launch around 2035, while SKAO, a giant radio telescope project being built in Australia and South Africa, could catch such waves by timing distant pulsars. Tests could come "as these facilities come online and begin data collection," Roshan said. A faint hum from the hot primordial plasma would carry the era's imprint too, but at frequencies beyond what existing detectors could pick up.

Andrey got his B.Sc. and M.Sc. degrees in elementary particle physics from Novosibirsk State University in Russia, and a Ph.D. in string theory from the Weizmann Institute of Science in Israel. He works as a science writer, specializing in physics, space, and technology. His articles have been published in AdvancedScienceNews, PhysicsWorld, Science, and other outlets.
There's a new type of landslide affecting northern latitudes, and it could affect more areas as the planet continues to warm.

These landslides, called permafrost detachment slides, occur in areas with relatively thin permafrost and seem to be a long-term impact of wildfire in these environments, according to a paper published Sept. 23 in the journal Geophysical Research Letters. Such slides have not been observed in the region before and may be unprecedented over the past 10,000 years or more, said study leader Joseph Young, who completed the work as part of his doctoral degree at the University of Alberta.
"It has been stable, and then it just flipped a switch, essentially," Young told Live Science.

Young and his colleagues were doing field observations in Canada's Northwest Territories when they noticed large landslide scars in valleys that have long hosted stable permafrost, which is sediment that remains frozen year-round. They began using satellite imagery to map the changes and also conducted fieldwork, which revealed that the slides weren't standard melting permafrost.

"Typically with permafrost, everything just thaws and melts in a slurry and moves like a mud downslope," Young said. "But with these large landslides, we found blocks of frozen material in the debris."

Some of these blocks were 33 feet (10 meters) tall, the height of a two-story house. The researchers ran an electrical current through the ground to determine the depth of the permafrost on the slopes.

They focused on two slides. One, in the Johnson River Valley, took place in 2017 and moved more than 636 million cubic feet (18 million cubic meters) of soil and rock. The other, in the Redstone River Valley, moved almost 159 million cubic feet (4.5 million cubic meters) of debris in 2018. The smaller slide left a scar three-quarters of a mile (1.2 kilometers) long, while the larger one gouged nearly 2 miles (3.2 km) out of the hillside.

The researchers then used the data they'd collected to build a model of how these icy slides occurred. The permafrost in this area has been warming by about 0.54 degrees Fahrenheit (0.3 degrees Celsius) per decade since 1980, when monitoring began, and there were also severe wildfires nearby in 1995.

The researchers found that instead of a top-down melting process by which the permafrost thawed to a muddy slurry from above, the slides were instead caused by a combination of fire-related thaw and warming temperatures, leading to cracks near the top of the slopes. These cracks allowed the thaw to penetrate deeper, eventually melting the bottom of the permafrost layer. This propagation can take 20 years to penetrate 66 feet (20 m), which is exactly what happened in the Johnson River and Redstone River valleys.
"We had a fire in '95 and then 20 years later, we start to get a lot of these widespread disturbances," Young said.

The two large slides the researchers studied are among more than 150 in the area, Young said. The others are smaller, but they still typically move over 35 million cubic feet (1 million cubic meters) of land apiece. Canada's Northwest Territories are remote, so the permafrost detachment slides have yet to damage any infrastructure. But the two in the study did dam rivers, creating brand-new lakes and rapidly dumping sediment into the waterways downstream, Young said.

There are many other places in Canada and Alaska where the permafrost is 66 to 130 feet (20 to 40 m) deep and thus vulnerable to the same type of slide. This is especially true given the increasing intensity of wildfire at northern latitudes, Young said.
"This is almost a potential glimpse into the future of what we might be able to expect in these areas with changing forest fire dynamics," he said.

More children, teens and very young adults are being diagnosed with colorectal cancer in the United States, and new research suggests they often experience aggressive forms of the disease.

While diagnosis rates are rising, the disease is still rare among young people. Colorectal cancer, which affects the lower intestines and rectum, is largely a disease of age: 55% of all colorectal cancers are diagnosed in people over 65, and only 16% occur in people ages 49 or younger, according to a 2026 study published in the flagship journal of the American Cancer Society. Only a few hundred cases per year are diagnosed in people under age 21 in the U.S.

Nevertheless, the numbers of cases in the very young are rising, even as colorectal cancer rates decline or hold steady in older individuals. This increase coincides with an overall rise in colon and rectal cancer rates in people under 50.

The reasons for this schism aren't entirely understood. People over 50 receive routine colonoscopies in which precancerous polyps are removed, and that likely accounts for much of the decline in colorectal cancer diagnoses in older adults. But researchers suspect that environmental factors, such as ultraprocessed foods and sedentary lifestyles, might be behind the growing rates in young people.

"Most of the research has really focused on the gut microbiome," the community of bacteria and other microbes that live in the gut, said Dr. Christopher Lieu, a professor of medical oncology at the University of Colorado Anschutz and a medical adviser to the nonprofit Colorectal Cancer Alliance.

Microbiome disruptions may spur inflammation, which, in turn, may trigger DNA mutations that cause cancer. But these mechanisms are complicated, Lieu told Live Science, and there likely isn't one simple reason young people's microbiomes may be getting disturbed.
"It's going to be extraordinarily more complex than that," he said.
What researchers are starting to learn is that colorectal cancer in people in their early 20s or younger tends to be a more aggressive disease than that often seen in older people.

"We do feel like it is a bit of a distinct disease than what we're seeing in older adults," said Dr. Erica Arnold, a pediatric surgery research fellow at Nationwide Children's Hospital in Columbus, Ohio. In October, Arnold presented new research on colorectal cancer in people ages 21 or younger at the annual meeting of the American Academy of Pediatrics.

Arnold and her colleagues analyzed the cases of 84 patients diagnosed between 2012 and 2023. They found that the median age of diagnosis was 16 years old and the median duration of symptoms before diagnosis was only 12 weeks long.
Only about 20% of the patients had a close relative with colorectal cancer, suggesting that for many of these young people, the disease did not necessarily emerge due to hereditary factors.

Eighty percent of the study participants were diagnosed with Stage III or Stage IV disease, meaning the cancer had already spread locally and to lymph nodes or to other, distant organs when the patients were diagnosed. For comparison, in colorectal cancer patients of all ages, 60% are diagnosed in Stage III or IV, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
In addition, Arnold said, one-third of the patients in their study had cellular markers of particularly aggressive cancer.
"Some of that might be related to delays in diagnosis," Lieu said, "but if you want my honest opinion, it does suggest that these cancers are developing differently."

The study's data was not nationally representative, but a recent analysis of CDC data has also found that colorectal cancer rates in youth are on the rise. In 1999, the diagnosis rate in kids ages 10 to 14 was 1 in a million. By 2020, it had risen to 6 in a million. For teens between 15 and 19, the rate of diagnosis went from 3 in a million to 13 in a million in that same time frame.

There is no definitive reason for this rise, Lieu said. Research on the microbiome has suggested that processed food, antibiotic exposure in childhood, stress, reduced exercise and other lifestyle factors may contribute to this increased risk of colorectal cancer.

Some microbes may play a particularly strong role, at least in some cases of colorectal cancer. For instance, a specific variant of the common gut bacterium Escherichia coli is strongly associated with colorectal cancer; the variant carries a genetic segment and produces compounds that are toxic to genes. But this variant alone cannot explain all colorectal cancer cases in young people. Nor is it clear why the gut microbiome might be undergoing a shift in the first place.
"It may be a combination of food, antibiotic use and environmental exposures," Lieu suggested.

Regardless of the exact causes behind the cases, Arnold's new research pointed to the symptoms that deserve closer scrutiny in young people. Among the 84 patients in the study, 75% reported experiencing back and abdominal pain before their diagnosis, 45% had changes in their bowel movements, 43% experienced unexplained weight loss and 38% had rectal bleeding.
These are classic colorectal cancer symptoms, Arnold said, but they might be overlooked in this young age group because these same symptoms can have more common causes.

Parents should know that in most cases, stomach pain and gastrointestinal disruptions in kids are not caused by colorectal cancer, Lieu said, calling the cancer an "extraordinarily rare event." Nevertheless, pain or gastrointestinal upset that doesn't ease or that worsens over time needs a checkup, and symptoms like weight loss and blood in the stool are very unusual in kids and deserve extra attention.
"It's just important to investigate it to make sure we're catching colorectal cancer earlier rather than later in these patients," Arnold said.

Numerous poll workers nationwide said they received confusing and sometimes contradictory orders from electoral authorities. Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin decided, minutes before polls closed, to extend all polling stations by two additional hours. By the time of the announcement, some polling centers had already closed, their voting machines had shut down, and they could not reopen. Fernnado Neisser, an electoral law professor at Fundação Getulio Vargas, a Brazilian research institute, said the election could be annulled if the margin is very narrow and it is shown that polling stations stayed open longer in areas that strongly favor one candidate.

A number of right-wing leaders have recently swept into power in Latin America, riding a wave of dissatisfaction with incumbent governments and deepening worries about security and a rising cost of living.

Until now, Brazil, the region’s largest nation, had been the exception. The left-wing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, began his third nonconsecutive term in 2023. His predecessor and rival, Jair Bolsonaro, had been convicted of trying to stage a coup to prevent Mr. Lula from taking office and was sentenced to 27 years, which he is currently serving under house arrest for health reasons.

Now Mr. Lula, weighed down by widespread perceptions of rising crime and economic woes, faces a challenge from the former president’s son, Flávio Bolsonaro, a right-wing senator. Mr. Bolsonaro’s formidable performance in the first voting round this month gave him the edge going into a two-way contest.
The outcome will have a profound effect on Brazil and its relations with the United States in particular. Here are some of the major issues at stake.
Mr. Bolsonaro has already said he would add Brazil to the Trump administration’s anti-cartel coalition, called the Shield of the Americas, and work with the United States to fight Brazilian gangs.

He suggested in social media posts last year that he would welcome U.S. military intervention in Brazil, though he denied that in recent interviews, saying the cooperation would be limited to intelligence. But it was Mr. Bolsonaro who successfully lobbied Mr. Trump to designate two Brazilian gangs as terrorist groups.
Mr. Lula has resisted joining the coalition, warning that intertwining too closely with the United States on security matters could threaten the nation’s sovereignty.

The Trump administration imposed tariffs on Brazilian products in an unsuccessful pressure campaign to disrupt the prosecution of Jair Bolsonaro. Many of those tariffs were eventually scaled back, and Brazil’s economy has remained largely unharmed by President Trump’s tariff campaign.

Another term for Mr. Lula, however, would increase the risk of more economic conflicts with the United States that might hurt the Brazilian economy. Of course, Mr. Bolsonaro would not be immune to those problems; Mr. Trump has been known to levy tariffs against allies as well as adversaries.

The Trump administration has signaled an interest in importing Brazilian oil to counter disruptions related to the Iran war and the country’s rare-earth minerals to reduce U.S. dependence on China for those resources. Mr. Bolsonaro is expected to align Brazil more closely with the United States than Mr. Lula has on trade issues, but neither leader can afford to anger China, a major trading partner.
The election could also affect Brazil’s ability to negotiate trade with the United States as a bloc with other countries in the region.

“Brazil’s relations with its neighbors have been extremely challenging,” said Carolina Moehlecke, an assistant professor of international relations at Getúlio Vargas Foundation, a research institution. This was especially true of its neighbor, Argentina, she added, whose right-wing president is a close ally of Mr. Trump. Mr. Bolsonaro, she said, might have an easier time cooperating with fellow right-wing leaders in Latin America.

If Mr. Bolsonaro carries the vote, conservationists fear a return to his father’s policies of allowing rapid deforestation in the Amazon rainforest, a trend that was largely reversed under President Lula. The younger Mr. Bolsonaro does not believe that climate change is caused by humans and has defended opening up protected lands to mining and farming.

He has also pledged to stem the nation’s rising debt. If he attempts to accomplish that through cuts to public spending, that could prove politically sensitive, Ms. Moehlecke said, especially when it comes to social welfare policies with broad popularity in Brazil. In the lead-up to Sunday’s elections, Mr. Lula had promised to increase welfare payments.

Mr. Lula has framed the election as a test of the nation’s democracy and portrays the Bolsonaros as a threat to democratic institutions. Ms. Moehlecke said it was likely Mr. Bolsonaro would take the country in a more authoritarian direction, though his rhetoric is generally tamer than his father’s.

But if Mr. Bolsonaro wins, his party’s gains in the legislature could allow him to deliver on some of his most polarizing promises: amnesty for his father, pardons for rioters who stormed Brazil’s halls of power after the last election, and a Senate more willing to try to remove justices who convicted his father.

If Mr. Lula wins, he most likely will face significant checks against his power. Right-wing candidates, including four other members of the Bolsonaro family, have made significant strides in the nation’s legislative races.

Oct. 26 (UPI) -- Chilean President José Antonio Kast is facing a severe political crisis following revelations that his government issued 56 administrative decrees reducing prison sentences for people convicted of sexually abusing and raping minors.

The Justice Ministry processed the sentence reductions between March and September 2026, triggering widespread public outrage, criticism from across the political spectrum and condemnation from Chile's Office of the Children's Ombudsman.
In response to the backlash, the Justice Ministry suspended the processing of additional sentence reductions.

The case was uncovered by Chilean news outlet Interferencia.cl, which obtained records showing that the decrees reduced sentences for 27 people convicted of sexual abuse and 29 convicted of rape. Several have already been released from prison.

Justice Minister Fernando Rabat argued that the decrees followed a legally established administrative procedure for inmates with good behavior who were sentenced before February 2022, when Law 21.421 restricted access to such benefits.

Rabat maintained that the Supreme Court required authorities to apply this criterion. However, news reports challenged his explanation, showing that the court had not mandated a uniform interpretation of the rules.

Opposition lawmakers demanded Rabat's resignation and announced preparations for possible impeachment proceedings. Kast reaffirmed his support for the minister Monday and tasked him with leading efforts to correct the situation and determine how the decisions were made.

"To those victims, to those children who are now young people or, in some cases, adults, and who are being forced to relive the worst moments of their lives, I say clearly that the state failed them," Kast said in an unexpected public statement.

"As the sitting president, I must assume the responsibility that falls on this government, which extends beyond the executive branch. We are taking responsibility, whatever the cost," he added, according to Chilean newspaper La Tercera.

Lawmakers from the governing Independent Democratic Union party called for the sentence reductions to be revoked, while Senate President Paulina Núñez of the National Renewal party announced plans for legislative changes.
"Laws must protect the most vulnerable people. Behind these crimes are victims and families who live with their consequences," Núñez said.
Roberto Mardones, director of the School of Government and Public Administration at Chile's Universidad Mayor, said the controversy threatens Kast's political identity and his ability to govern.

"Clearly, there is a potentially very high political cost here because this decision affects two of Kast's central promises. On the one hand, there is security, and on the other, the protection of children and families," Mardones told UPI.

The controversy also comes as Kast prepares to grant humanitarian pardons to former military officers convicted of human rights violations committed during the dictatorship of Augusto Pinochet, a measure he had promised during his election campaign.
Mardones said the controversy raises questions about the consistency of Kast's political message and his government's ability to act in accordance with its stated priorities.

"There is a high political risk that some citizens will conclude that the government is not delivering on its promises and that its concrete decisions are not fulfilling the commitment to protection that underpinned his campaign," he said.
The crisis coincides with declining public approval of the president.
According to the latest Plaza Pública survey by polling firm Cadem, released Sunday, Kast's approval rating fell 4 percentage points to 29%, while his disapproval rating rose 4 points to 66%.
The survey found that 89% of respondents were aware of the controversy and 92% opposed the sentence reductions, regardless of the legal arguments used to justify them. Only 3% supported the measures.

Kast's government has faced a series of political and communications setbacks during its eight months in office, including the elimination of fuel subsidies and the dismissal of the security minister and government spokesperson less than three months after they took office because of poor performance. Those episodes have damaged the administration's public image.

"There is already a basis for saying that this is a serious controversy amid the ongoing erosion of support for this government, and it could reinforce the perception of a pattern of poorly anticipated decisions and corrections made under pressure," Mardones said.

Oct. 26 (UPI) -- The former personal assistant of comedian Russell Brand told a court Monday about her experience working for him, saying he had an "insane sexual appetite" and that he would ask her to get phone numbers for him from female fans.

Helen Berger worked for Brand from June 2006 to February 2007. Brand, 51, is accused of three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one charge of indecent assault. Six women made the accusations, which span 10 years starting in 1999.
Berger's written statement, read Monday in Southwark Crown Court, said that she never saw Brand do anything against the law but that she did see him "treat women poorly."

"Though I'd worked with celebrities before and seen a lot of people normalizing bad behavior, this was on another level," she said. "I think everyone else normalizing and dismissing Russell's behavior made me think, I guess, this is just the way it is."
Berger made her statement to police in May 2024. She said she left her job with Brand because she was burnt out and "sick of him."

Berger describes an environment in which Brand had sex with numerous women during her time as his assistant, saying that he found random women online to sleep with and that she once had to stop his mother and girlfriend from walking in on him while he was having sex with someone in his dressing room.
She said his requests for female fans' phone numbers made her "uncomfortable" and that she stopped doing so.
Prosecution statements Monday also included one from the manager of a woman who said Brand sexually assaulted her when she worked for Channel 4 in 2009.

The manager said the woman told her that Jack Bayles and Gareth Roy, Brand's associates, told her she had to give Brand a massage or he would not continue with the day's recording. The manager also reported that the woman said Bayles and Roy were present and "watched and laughed" while Brand "sexually assaulted her right in front of them."

Their call came as they released a 53-page staff report entitled "'We Have Certain Things in Common, Jeffrey," probing the alleged links between the late financier and President Donald Trump and accusing the president's Department of Justice of systematically suppressing the evidence in the FBI's "Epstein Files."
"Donald Trump says he knew Jeffrey Epstein 'just like everybody in Palm Beach knew him,'" ranking committee member Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., said in a statement.
"Not exactly. Evidence involving 11 women tells a completely different and far more damning story about their relationship and the abuse of young women and girls that took place in their network."
Raskin urged that Attorney General Todd Blanche appoint a special counsel to dig into the matter.

"The women who survived Epstein deserve to be heard, Congress must have the complete files required by law, and an independent special counsel must investigate Epstein's co-conspirators and DOJ's cover-up and ensure that state and foreign prosecutors have the evidence they need to pursue justice," he said.
Trump has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing in connection with Epstein's sex crimes, asserting the two former friends became estranged long ago and that he subsequently banned Epstein from Mar-a-Lago.

The majority of Volkswagen vehicles sold in the past decade have electronic parking brakes. However, most customers don’t even realize that the vehicle has an electronic parking brake, because the system engages and disengages the parking brake automatically on most vehicles. But, when the system fails and turns on the light or has a warning in the driver information center, then the customer will notice.

If you are doing a brake job on a vehicle with an electronic parking brake, you will need a scan tool with the proper software for the parking brake system to retract the calipers, adjust and perform diagnostics. There are no shortcuts on YouTube. You can find videos that involve removing the electric motor, jumping connectors and disassembling the parking brake mechanism. But, these methods are very risky and can damage the vehicle and kill productivity. Unapproved methods will set malfunction codes, and the worst-case scenario is that you could damage the unit.
The VW system that was installed on many of its platforms starting in 2004 is an example of a system that requires a scan tool to replace the rear brake pads.

The system has stepper motors on the back of the caliper that actuate the piston. The motor can be removed from the caliper, though the ignition should be switched off for at least 30 seconds before removing the connector.

The motor is sealed to the caliper with an o-ring around the spindle. The condition of this o-ring is critical for the life of the motor and should be lightly lubricated with brake fluid. If the o-ring fails, water and debris will be one step closer to the motor gears.
The spindle on the caliper can be rocked slightly with a torx bit so the motor seats in the spindle. Don’t force the motor assembly onto the caliper, because damage to the housing can occur.

On recent platforms, VW have outfitted the motors with a sensor that can measure brake pad wear and adjust the pads for the least amount of drag. During this adjustment on some vehicles, the pad thickness is calculated. The system counts the number of rotations of the motor with a hall effect sensor inside the unit.
Inspecting the caliper, hardware and motors may not give you a complete picture of what is happening with these systems. Having access to a scan tool can reduce diagnostic time.

The OEMs have built-in bi-directional protocols to retract the parking brake so the pads can be replaced. A dedicated brake tool or enhanced scan tool is able to command these protocols and interrogate the module for codes and faults.

The Electronic Parking Brake Module (EPBM) is the module on the CAN bus of most vehicles equipped with this system. Any missing data for vehicle speed, gear position or brake pedal input will cause a problem with the system.

Some systems use information from the electric parking brake to track shoe and pad wear. The system will count the number of turns the actuator makes or the position of the stepper motor to determine the thickness of the friction material.

If you do find yourself working on a vehicle whose electronic parking brake will not disengage, the first thing to do is look at the basics. Some systems require that the doors be shut and the brake pedal depressed. Some models may even require the seat belt to be buckled. Simple items like a defective brake pedal or door switch may hinder operation. Also, in some cases, the button may be defective. On some vehicles, the operation of the switch can be verified with a scan tool.

More than 700 NAPA Auto Care centers nationwide participate in the program, which combines technical education, hands-on experience and mentorship. Its mission is to educate and cultivate the next generation of automotive repair professionals by providing a broad learning experience that combines online and classroom training.

For shop owners, the program offers an alternative to waiting for experienced technicians to appear in an increasingly competitive labor market. A participating shop can identify someone with the right attitude and work ethic, then help that person build technical skills through a defined training path.

“NAPA is committed to finding solutions that address the national shortage of skilled automotive technicians,” said Jason Rainey, vice president of Auto Care. “Our apprenticeship program is one of several key NAPA initiatives that help pave the way for young people to launch long and fruitful careers in our industry.”

The NAPA Apprentice Program uses a nine-stage curriculum designed to give participants a broad understanding of the systems and components found on modern vehicles. Most apprentices can complete the program in two years or less.

However, the curriculum is competency-based rather than tied strictly to a calendar. Apprentices can progress through each stage at a pace that matches their learning style and demonstrated abilities. A participant who quickly masters a subject can move forward, while someone who needs additional practice can spend more time developing that competency.
Training is 100% technical and is delivered through several formats:
- Classroom training videos exclusive to the Apprentice Program provide in-depth instruction from experienced master technicians.
- NAPA Autotech classes offer instructor-led training taught by experienced ASE Master Certified instructors.
- Autotech eLearning provides web-based instruction targeting specific systems, procedures and diagnostic topics.
- Hands-on training allows apprentices to apply what they have learned while working in the shop under the guidance of a mentor.

This combination helps connect classroom theory with real repairs. Apprentices do not just learn how a component operates; they also gain experience inspecting, testing and servicing that component on vehicles.

The curriculum will continue to evolve as vehicle technology and industry standards change. Planned enhancements include updated training modules and specialized certification options covering emerging service areas, giving apprentices additional opportunities for career advancement.

Apprentices earn the work experience requirement for three Automotive Service Excellence certifications as they advance through the program: Maintenance and Light Repair (G1), Suspension and Steering (A4), and Brakes (A5). They also gain the practical know-how to pass the EPA Section 609 refrigerant recovery and recycling credential test administered through ASE.

That distinction is important: G1, A4 and A5 are ASE professional certifications, while Section 609 is an EPA-required credential for technicians who service motor-vehicle air-conditioning systems. Together, these credentials provide outside validation of the knowledge and skills developed during the apprenticeship.

Because the program is registered with the U.S. Department of Labor, graduates also finish with a nationally recognized journey-level credential in automotive repair. This gives apprentices evidence of completing a structured combination of education and supervised on-the-job training.

The program provides the curriculum and training materials, but its success inside a repair facility depends heavily on the shop’s involvement. An apprentice needs an experienced technician who can explain procedures, demonstrate good work habits, supervise repairs and provide constructive feedback.

“We need their mentorship, their participation,” said Hannah Klausman, account marketing manager for Auto Care. “We want to support them by providing the materials for their technicians to go through this program, but we need their buy-in by having them provide a mentor and really put their time into taking a chance on these new technicians.”

For a shop owner, that requires a real commitment. Mentoring can temporarily affect the productivity of an experienced technician, especially during an apprentice’s first months. The potential return is a technician trained around the shop’s procedures, quality standards and culture.

The program can also create a clearer career ladder. Instead of hiring someone as an entry-level employee with no defined next step, a shop can show the apprentice how training, demonstrated competencies and certifications lead to greater responsibilities.

“The success of the apprentice program is a reflection not only of the investment NAPA has made but also of its collaboration with Auto Care centers across the country,” said Ryan Ouellette, director of strategic accounts at NAPA. “We are committed to developing future professionals at NAPA, and we look forward to continuing to educate and support the talent in the industry.”
Applicants must be at least 17 years old. Applicants who are 17 require written parental consent, and there is no maximum age.

Previous professional repair experience is not the program’s defining qualification. Shops should look for candidates who have a positive attitude, arrive ready to work and take initiative beyond their assigned tasks.

Successful apprentices must also be able to build relationships. Automotive repair is increasingly collaborative, particularly when diagnostic information, specialized equipment and technical knowledge must be shared among technicians. An apprentice must be willing to ask questions, accept coaching and learn from the people around them.
Most importantly, candidates need to embrace continuous learning. Vehicle technology does not stand still, and neither can a technician’s education.

For aspiring technicians, the program provides an opportunity to learn the trade without taking on the expense of a traditional trade-school program. Apprentices receive a paycheck while learning in an operating repair facility, and the training itself is provided at no cost to the participant.
Additional information about the program is available at NAPA Auto Care Training.

Preparing for an Automotive Service Excellence (ASE) certification exam takes more than memorizing terms and reviewing repair procedures. You need to understand how vehicle systems work, recognize diagnostic clues and apply your knowledge when the answer isn’t immediately obvious.

The good news? Many of the skills that make you a better technician can also make you a stronger test-taker. With a solid study plan and the right approach to practice questions, you can head into your ASE exam ready to tackle the challenges ahead.

Before opening a textbook or watching a training video, identify which ASE test you’re preparing to take. Each exam focuses on specific systems and service procedures, so knowing what to expect helps you use your study time effectively.
Review the official ASE study guides and task lists to identify the topics covered. Then compare those topics with your current knowledge and hands-on experience.

For example, if you’re preparing for the A6 Electrical/Electronic Systems test, you might feel comfortable testing batteries and charging systems but need additional practice interpreting wiring diagrams. Spend more time on the topics that challenge you instead of repeatedly reviewing material you already know.
Practice Thinking Through Diagnostic Questions
ASE exams aren’t just about recalling facts. Many questions present a vehicle symptom or service problem and ask you to identify the most likely cause or appropriate diagnostic step.

Imagine a vehicle arrives with a battery that repeatedly goes dead overnight. You might immediately suspect a failing battery. But what if the charging system operates correctly and the battery passes its tests?

A good technician considers other possibilities, including an excessive parasitic draw. That same diagnostic thinking helps you work through ASE-style questions.Read each question carefully, identify the relevant symptoms and evaluate the available answers. Don’t jump to conclusions based on one familiar detail.
One of the most useful ASE test-taking skills is recognizing why an answer doesn’t fit.
When facing a multiple-choice question, start by identifying what the question is actually asking. Is it looking for the most likely cause, the next diagnostic step or the correct repair procedure?

Next, eliminate answers that conflict with the symptoms or accepted service procedures. Even when you’re unsure of the correct response, narrowing your choices can improve your chances of selecting the right answer.
This approach is especially helpful with Technician A and Technician B questions, which require you to evaluate two separate statements before choosing an answer.
Use Video Training and Practice Tests Together
Different study methods reinforce different skills. Reading helps you review technical information, while videos can make complicated procedures easier to understand.

The free ASE Study Center offers video-based instruction and ASE-style practice questions to help technicians prepare. Its training modules focus on test-related topics and encourage learners to understand the reasoning behind correct answers.
Instead of simply watching a video and moving on, pause and explain the procedure in your own words. Then use practice questions to check whether you can apply what you’ve learned.
When you miss a question, review the explanation. Understanding why an answer is incorrect can teach you just as much as getting one right.

Knowing the material is important, but managing your time matters, too. ASE certification exams are timed, making it useful to practice answering questions without spending too long on any single problem.

Try completing a set of practice questions under timed conditions. Review your results afterward and identify whether mistakes came from unfamiliar material, misreading questions or second-guessing yourself.
As test day approaches, focus on reviewing weak areas, getting adequate rest and arriving prepared to concentrate.
Turn Test Preparation Into Shop-Ready Skills
ASE preparation should do more than help you pass an exam. It should strengthen the habits you’ll use every day in the service bay.
Learning to identify symptoms, eliminate incorrect possibilities and verify your conclusions makes you a more capable technician.

The next time you face a challenging practice question, approach it like a vehicle diagnosis: Gather the facts, think through the problem and trust the process. Those are skills worth carrying well beyond test day.

Caster tire wear is usually indirect, but the alignment angle can influence how tread wears during turns. It is one of the fundamental wheel alignment angles, and while it does not directly cause tire wear, it can affect shoulder loading during cornering.
Caster is the angle of the steering axis when viewed from the side of the vehicle. That axis acts as the hinge line around which the wheel pivots when the driver turns the steering wheel.

Most vehicles use positive caster. This means the top of the steering axis tilts slightly toward the rear of the vehicle. Positive caster helps the steering return to center after a turn. It also improves straight-line stability, especially at highway speeds.
Caster Tire Wear Develops Through Camber Change
Caster changes how the wheels lean during a turn. With positive caster, the inner wheel tilts outward while the outer wheel tilts inward.
This movement shifts load across the tire contact patches and helps the vehicle corner.

Caster does not normally wear a tire by itself. Instead, it changes camber as the wheels turn, a movement often called camber roll. As the tires lean during cornering, more load can be placed on the tread shoulders. Under normal driving, the effect may be minor. Aggressive cornering, however, can accelerate shoulder wear.
Too much caster can also make steering feel heavy or harsh. For that reason, caster specifications vary by vehicle.
For tire dealers and alignment technicians, caster may not be the direct cause of an unusual wear pattern. However, it can contribute to shoulder wear by changing wheel angle during turns.
Changes to the California Bureau of Automotive Repair (BAR) storage fee and airbag safety regulations are expected to take effect Jan. 1, pending approval by the Office of Administrative Law (OAL).
BAR also plans to change its towing authorization regulations, with a comment period open Oct. 30-Dec. 14.

BAR says the storage fee changes clarify how and when automotive repair dealers (ARDs) can charge the fees. Adopted changes to airbag regulations would expand repair safety in the state, including requiring ARDs to follow OEM procedures, according to BAR.
In an update given at BAR’s Advisory Group meeting on Oct. 22, the adopted storage fee changes would require ARDs to:
- Store a vehicle at its primary business address as registered with BAR;
- Provide an itemized invoice for storage fees;
- Post current daily storage fees in an area frequented by customers; and
- Report maximum daily storage rate to BAR when renewing registration.
Based on reported daily storage rates, BAR plans to launch a search tool on its website that shows the average and median rates using defined geographic areas around each ARD.

BAR held four public workshops on proposed changes, which were modified at least twice. Three comment periods were also held. BAR submitted its package on the changes to the OAL on Oct. 9 for final approval. BAR said last week the OAL deadline is Nov. 23.

The OAL previously identified several provisions where wording needed greater clarity to ensure consistent interpretation and application. In August, BAR said it withdrew the package to address the concerns.

The passage of AB1263 in 2024 gave BAR authority to address storage fees. It also allows BAR to codify its guidance and unify existing laws on the subject, which BAR says is part of the regulation changes package. The changes also include teardown disclosures.
Repairers have previously voiced concerns about language in the proposed regulations that would cap storage fees and cause shops to lose storage revenue.

Under the airbag safety regulation changes, ARDs will be required “to restore an airbag that is part of an inflatable restraint system to its original operating condition as designed by the original equipment manufacturer (OEM).”

Prohibit an ARD from manufacturing, installing, or selling any airbag or airbag part/component that has been deployed, has an electrical fault, includes a component designed to mislead the vehicle owner or operator into believing a functional airbag has been installed, or displays a mark identical or substantially similar to the genuine mark of a motor vehicle manufacturer, or a parts supplier without authorization from the OEM or supplier.
ARDs would also not be allowed to manufacture, install, or sell recalled airbags either by the OEM or the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration.
BAR states that ARDs can buy airbag replacement parts or components from OEMs; suppliers or resellers previously authorized by the appropriate OEM; or DMV-licensed automotive dismantlers.
The California Department of Consumer Affairs is reviewing the package. After that’s complete, BAR says it will file the package with OAL for final approval.

Proposed towing authorization changes would require customer authorization for towing fees before service on a separate document from repair authorizations. ARDs would also have to list any storage or towing-related charges as separate line items on the invoice. The package has been filed with the OAL.
The Advisory Group also received an update last week on BAR consumer complaints data.
Complaints have increased about 15% over the past year, with auto body making up 16% of all complaints. Engine repair complaints were highest at 35%.
